Prohibition. The period from nineteen twenty to nineteen thirty-three when the United States banned the production, importation, transportation, and sale of alcoholic beverages, enforced by the Volstead Act. Intended by reformers as moral and public-health legislation, Prohibition instead created a vast underground economy, fueled organized crime, and ultimately failed due to lack of public support and the vast gap between law and popular practice. Its repeal via the twenty-first Amendment stands as the only time the U.S. Constitution reversed a previous amendment, marking a pivotal moment in American political culture and the limits of federal regulatory power.

Prohibition was championed by progressive reformers, religious groups, and women's organizations as a solution to alcoholism, poverty, and violence. It passed with overwhelming congressional support after decades of advocacy by the Anti-Saloon League and temperance movements. The eighteenth Amendment, ratified in nineteen nineteen, and the Volstead Act established Prohibition. Enforcement fell to a vastly underfunded federal Prohibition Bureau with only fifteen hundred agents attempting to police a nation of over one hundred million, making effective enforcement essentially impossible.

Rather than eliminating alcohol consumption, Prohibition created speakeasies—illegal bars—bootleg production, smuggling networks, and criminal syndicates. Organized crime figures like Al Capone became enormously profitable and powerful, gaining social and political influence. The Noble Experiment disproportionately affected the poor and working class, who consumed illegally produced and often dangerous liquor, while the wealthy accessed smuggled quality products through private clubs and personal connections to bootleggers.

Prohibition overlapped with and energized the Harlem Renaissance and the Jazz Age. Speakeasies became centers of jazz music, African American culture, and social transgression in Northern cities, driving nightlife and cultural innovation during the nineteen twenties. The apparent hypocrisy of Prohibition—widespread law-breaking sanctioned by the government's own unrealistic law—undermined faith in government institutions and contributed to widespread moral relativism that persisted through the Depression and beyond. Repeal came through the twenty-first Amendment, ratified in nineteen thirty-three, after years of growing opposition, becoming a cautionary lesson about the limits of federal regulatory power over deeply entrenched social practices.
